news.title: Civil Society Groups to House: Support Every Article of Impeachment for Hegseth
news.description: On Tuesday, a coalition of more than 40 civil society organizations sent a letter calling on all House members to vote for every article of impeachment filed against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. On Monday, Rep. Thomas Massie filed the eight articles and the House is expected to begin voting on them Tuesday evening. In their letter, the groups called out Hegseth’s prosecution of the unauthorized Iran war, his approval of lethal military strikes on fishing boats and his unprecedented political attacks on Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) as reasons to support impeachment. Read the Letter The letter demands that members defend Congress’s constitutional authority consistently including in Iran, Venezuela, the boat strikes and Yemen, regardless of members’ views on the politics of any particular operation. The coalition behind the letter include Demand Progress, MoveOn, OxFam America, Public Citizen and 39 other organizations. “Pete Hegseth’s time at the Pentagon has done grievous harm to the nation and to the Constitution,” said Demand progress Senior Policy Advisor Cavan Kharrazian. “This is a man who ignored the will of Congress to execute an illegal war in Iran, kidnapped a foreign leader for oil, restarted war on Yemen, sent missiles to kill suspected drug traffickers and weaponized the Pentagon against a political enemy. Every House member who cares about the Constitution must vote for every single article of impeachment filed against Pete Hegseth.” “Congress never authorized the war with Iran,” stated the letter. “Secretary Hegseth directed U.S. forces into hostilities in violation of the Constitution and the War Powers Resolution. Both chambers went further and adopted H. Con. Res. 86, directing the President to withdraw U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran. The Pentagon continued the war anyway. A vote to impeach would affirm that a defense secretary can be held accountable for carrying on a war Congress never authorized and expressly called on the President to end.”

news.title: Bernie Sanders Warns Chuck Schumer His Days as Senate Leader Are Up
news.description: Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders has added his name to the growing list of liberal-minded lawmakers asking Chuck Schumer to hand over the reins of the Senate. Sanders told reporters Tuesday that he would not support Schumer’s bid for Senate majority leader in the new year. When asked by The Washington Times’s Lindsey McPherson if he would support Schumer even if the current leader runs unopposed, Sanders responded: “He’s not going to run unopposed, I don’t think.” A wave of Democratic voices opposing Schumer’s possible return atop the Senate emerged after the party won an overwhelming majority in Congress last week, rebuking the septuagenarian’s establishment politics. In the days since, Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has emerged as a potential alternative, indicating a rising interest in progressive leadership. Van Hollen rose as a leading progressive last year, when he travelled out of the country to visit his constituent Kilmar Ábrego García after he was illegally deported by the Trump administration to El Salvador’s notoriously lethal maximum security prison, CECOT. Whether or not Van Hollen will officially commit himself against Schumer remains to be seen, though the Marylander has already started to draft an opposition platform that could put pressure on Schumer’s politics. On Tuesday, Van Hollen declared that the U.S. cannot spend “a penny more” on the Iran War, daring Donald Trump to either stop funding the war or face the possibility of a government shutdown. So far, at least nine major politicos have either peeled away from Schumer outright or indicated an interest in a different Senate majority leader. They include: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal Illinois Senator-elect Juliana Stratton Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan Kansas Senator-elect Adam Hamilton Maine Senator-elect Troy Jackson New Hampshire Senator-elect Chris Pappas Texas Senator-elect James Talarico Another 14 senators or senators-elect have not yet committed as to whether or not they will support Schumer, according to an analysis published Monday by Primary Democrats. Altogether, that’s 23 Democrats—or nearly half of the at least 54 Democratic seats that will dominate the upper chamber come January. New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has also refused to support her home state senator, though the decision is ultimately up to the Senate.

news.title: Local Republicans caught in Trump's crossfire in a high-stakes panic
news.description: In analyzing a landslide midterm election, most of the focus has rightly been on the American South. However, there are lessons to be learned elsewhere. After Democrat Troy Jackson defeated Susan Collins in Maine, there will be no Republican senators from New England next year. In fact, no state in the region – Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Connecticut – will send any Republicans to the US Congress, either to the Senate or the House of Representatives. There is only one exception. Maine is sending former Governor Paul LePage to the House to represent its 2nd Congressional district. The Boston Globe called that fact “supremely ironic.” Though the midterms were a wholesale rebuke of the president and what he stands for, “LePage claims he was Donald Trump before there was Donald Trump. LePage likes to threaten people and routinely says outrageous, bigoted things. He and his hero are like peas and carrots.” New England and the South are inverse reflections. The South used to be home of the slavers. The Democrats were their primary vehicle. New England used to be home of the abolitionists. The Republicans were theirs. (The GOP arose from the ashes of the Whig Party to gain power with Abraham Lincoln’s victory in 1865.) Each region flipped over time as the country fought over the role of minority rights and freedoms in national politics, especially those of Black Americans. The South moved from blue to red. There were zero Democratic senators by 2015. New England moved from red to blue. There will be zero Republican senators by 2027, completing a process begun over 160 years ago. The bluing of New England didn’t stop at the federal level. While Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota and Nevada saw their state governments flip from partial control to total control by the Democrats, here in Connecticut, for instance, the Democratic Party was already the majority. Thanks to Donald Trump, however, state and local Republicans are being driven to despair. Next year, the state Senate will have the largest Democratic majority in 140 years, the Register said. For the party, that’s more than at any time in state history. Of the 36 seats in the state Senate, either 32 or 33 will be Democrats (one election is pending). There will be either three or four GOP Senators. Meanwhile, the state House will have the biggest Democratic majority since 1975 – since Watergate. Of the 151 state House seats, as many as 118 will be Democrats. Connecticut Governor Ned Lamont did more than become the second to win three consecutive terms. He won with the largest margins by a Democrat since Watergate. His first margin was three points. His second, 13. His third, 18. You could argue that Ned Lamont has been touched by an angel. Every time he campaigned for governor, Donald Trump was in the background. Just 10 years ago the Connecticut Senate was tied, 18-18. In 2016, the state House had 79 Democrats and 72 Republicans (then out of a total of 150). What happened during that decade-plus? Trump happened. He destroyed the Connecticut GOP. Connecticut Republicans are going to be in the same pickle that Republicans in other states will be in – between a past chained to Trump and a hoped-for future unchained from him. One big problem is rightwing media and rightwing organizations. Despite Tuesday’s crushing defeat, they continue to punish Republicans office holders for disloyalty while making it impossible for them to distance themselves from the most unpopular president since Herbert Hoover. A leading Republican in Arizona called Turning Point USA, the group founded by the late demagogue Charlie Kirk, “a destructive force” that’s “driving us to extinction,” comparing it to a parasite that is slowly killing its host. A leading Republican in the New York State Assembly, after watching GOP-held offices turn blue and the number of US congresspeople erode from seven to six (out of 26), said that the New York Republican Party needs “an enema.” Of course, the main problem is Trump. The Republicans were routed in part by a Hispanic backlash against his murderous deportation program. Yet Friday, he promoted Stephen Miller, the architect of the purge. Meanwhile, the president is trying to hold his fracturing coalition together by threatening its component parts. In a memo last week to more than 3,000 rightwing groups, the White House attacked Republicans who blamed Trump for the midterm wipeout, adding that “we are monitoring statements, press releases, and media engagements from your organizations.” At some point you would expect self-preservation to kick in, and perhaps we are seeing something like that from Ron Johnson. Earlier this year, after the murders of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, he opposed Democratic efforts to put limits on ICE. After the midterms, however, the senator from Wisconsin said there is corruption “within the Trump administration.” He didn’t call out Trump, only unnamed White House aides allegedly catering to corporate interests, not the people’s interests. Johnson is up for reelection in 2028. He said his party must “embrace the enduring principles of our founders, limited government.” If Johnson is going to win reelection in a state that’s gone totally Democratic, he has to convince Wisconsinites that he was never the authoritarian he really did make himself out to be, but instead a “constitutional conservative” the whole time. To do that, however, he has to walk the same tightrope every Republican in every blue state must walk. He must persuade Republican voters that he’s still loyal to Trump and everyone else that he doesn’t carry his stink. The midterms completed a long process in New England. We used to be solid red. One hundred and sixty-one years later, we are solid blue (with one “supremely ironic” exception). Meanwhile, the midterms seem to have begun a new phase in the politics of the south, where there has not been a Democratic US senator in eight years. Now there’s going to four (presuming Mississippi goes Scott Colom’s way). Trump broke the Solid South. Meanwhile, New England is closed. Other regions are closing. In 2012, Barack Obama talked about a future in which the fever that gripped the GOP after his 2008 election would break. I don’t want to get ahead of myself, but maybe it’s breaking.

news.title: Ejected GOP senator teases ‘suspense’ as Trump nominee’s fate hangs in the balance
news.description: Donald Trump’s pick to replace Dr. Marty Makary as head of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) could end up a casualty of Republican anger over Trump’s role in the GOP’s midterm massacre. Heidi Overton’s path to confirmation was already narrow, and the Washington Sun reported it’s getting narrower by the day. Her biggest problem is the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, where she needs every Republican vote. Two of those Republicans, Chair Bill Cassidy (R-LA) and Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME), are lame ducks who just lost their seats and may feel little obligation to do Trump favors, the Sun reported. Cassidy offered no hints. “You gotta wait, man, suspense,” he told reporters Monday. Pressed on whether he had reservations about Overton, he replied, “No comment.” Cassidy, a doctor and vaccine supporter, was knocked out in his primary by Trump-endorsed Julia Letlow. He has warned before that he might block Trump’s health nominees over the administration’s vaccine policies, though he has yet to vote against one. Collins lost her bid for a sixth term to Democrat Troy Jackson last week and has refused to say how she will vote. Abortion could be a sticking point, the report notes. At her confirmation hearing, Overton avoided committing to a position on the FDA’s review of the abortion pill mifepristone. Collins, who supports abortion rights, cited Attorney General Todd Blanche’s stance on abortion as one reason she voted against him. Time is also against Overton. Republicans are trying to squeeze dozens of nominees through before Democrats take control of the Senate in January. Add to that, the Sun reported, "Overton lost an advocate in the White House with the departure of former chief of staff Susie Wiles." If she isn’t confirmed, the FDA’s leadership will stay in limbo. Kyle Diamantas has been acting commissioner since Makary was forced out last spring. According to a senior administration official, the White House would then put Sara Brenner, a former top FDA deputy who now leads the White House pandemic preparedness office, in charge. The report notes that Trump reportedly had first asked Diamantas to take the job permanently, but he declined, saying "he wants to leave by year’s end" to spend more time with his young family.

news.title: Local Republicans caught in Trump's crossfire in a high-stakes panic
news.description: In analyzing a landslide midterm election, most of the focus has rightly been on the American South. However, there are lessons to be learned elsewhere. After Democrat Troy Jackson defeated Susan Collins in Maine, there will be no Republican senators from New England next year. In fact, no state in the region – Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Connecticut – will send any Republicans to the US Congress, either to the Senate or the House of Representatives. There is only one exception. Maine is sending former Governor Paul LePage to the House to represent its 2nd Congressional district. The Boston Globe called that fact “supremely ironic.” Though the midterms were a wholesale rebuke of the president and what he stands for, “LePage claims he was Donald Trump before there was Donald Trump. LePage likes to threaten people and routinely says outrageous, bigoted things. He and his hero are like peas and carrots.” New England and the South are inverse reflections. The South used to be home of the slavers. The Democrats were their primary vehicle. New England used to be home of the abolitionists. The Republicans were theirs. (The GOP arose from the ashes of the Whig Party to gain power with Abraham Lincoln’s victory in 1865.) Each region flipped over time as the country fought over the role of minority rights and freedoms in national politics, especially those of Black Americans. The South moved from blue to red. There were zero Democratic senators by 2015. New England moved from red to blue. There will be zero Republican senators by 2027, completing a process begun over 160 years ago. The bluing of New England didn’t stop at the federal level. While Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota and Nevada saw their state governments flip from partial control to total control by the Democrats, here in Connecticut, for instance, the Democratic Party was already the majority. Thanks to Donald Trump, however, state and local Republicans are being driven to despair. Next year, the state Senate will have the largest Democratic majority in 140 years, the Register said. For the party, that’s more than at any time in state history. Of the 36 seats in the state Senate, either 32 or 33 will be Democrats (one election is pending). There will be either three or four GOP Senators. Meanwhile, the state House will have the biggest Democratic majority since 1975 – since Watergate. Of the 151 state House seats, as many as 118 will be Democrats. Connecticut Governor Ned Lamont did more than become the second to win three consecutive terms. He won with the largest margins by a Democrat since Watergate. His first margin was three points. His second, 13. His third, 18. You could argue that Ned Lamont has been touched by an angel. Every time he campaigned for governor, Donald Trump was in the background. Just 10 years ago the Connecticut Senate was tied, 18-18. In 2016, the state House had 79 Democrats and 72 Republicans (then out of a total of 150). What happened during that decade-plus? Trump happened. He destroyed the Connecticut GOP. Connecticut Republicans are going to be in the same pickle that Republicans in other states will be in – between a past chained to Trump and a hoped-for future unchained from him. One big problem is rightwing media and rightwing organizations. Despite Tuesday’s crushing defeat, they continue to punish Republicans office holders for disloyalty while making it impossible for them to distance themselves from the most unpopular president since Herbert Hoover. A leading Republican in Arizona called Turning Point USA, the group founded by the late demagogue Charlie Kirk, “a destructive force” that’s “driving us to extinction,” comparing it to a parasite that is slowly killing its host. A leading Republican in the New York State Assembly, after watching GOP-held offices turn blue and the number of US congresspeople erode from seven to six (out of 26), said that the New York Republican Party needs “an enema.” Of course, the main problem is Trump. The Republicans were routed in part by a Hispanic backlash against his murderous deportation program. Yet Friday, he promoted Stephen Miller, the architect of the purge. Meanwhile, the president is trying to hold his fracturing coalition together by threatening its component parts. In a memo last week to more than 3,000 rightwing groups, the White House attacked Republicans who blamed Trump for the midterm wipeout, adding that “we are monitoring statements, press releases, and media engagements from your organizations.” At some point you would expect self-preservation to kick in, and perhaps we are seeing something like that from Ron Johnson. Earlier this year, after the murders of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, he opposed Democratic efforts to put limits on ICE. After the midterms, however, the senator from Wisconsin said there is corruption “within the Trump administration.” He didn’t call out Trump, only unnamed White House aides allegedly catering to corporate interests, not the people’s interests. Johnson is up for reelection in 2028. He said his party must “embrace the enduring principles of our founders, limited government.” If Johnson is going to win reelection in a state that’s gone totally Democratic, he has to convince Wisconsinites that he was never the authoritarian he really did make himself out to be, but instead a “constitutional conservative” the whole time. To do that, however, he has to walk the same tightrope every Republican in every blue state must walk. He must persuade Republican voters that he’s still loyal to Trump and everyone else that he doesn’t carry his stink. The midterms completed a long process in New England. We used to be solid red. One hundred and sixty-one years later, we are solid blue (with one “supremely ironic” exception). Meanwhile, the midterms seem to have begun a new phase in the politics of the south, where there has not been a Democratic US senator in eight years. Now there’s going to four (presuming Mississippi goes Scott Colom’s way). Trump broke the Solid South. Meanwhile, New England is closed. Other regions are closing. In 2012, Barack Obama talked about a future in which the fever that gripped the GOP after his 2008 election would break. I don’t want to get ahead of myself, but maybe it’s breaking.
